original_claim_summary: All federal DEI officers were allegedly fired overnight on January 20, 2025, with hundreds losing their jobs immediately.

source_urls.access_notes: Reuters article text retrieved; reports the January 21 OPM memo and next-day deadlines.
supports: OPM directed agencies to place DEI office staff on paid leave by 5 p.m. January 22 and prepare reduction-in-force plans.
The report describes a process to dismantle offices and plan layoffs, not same-night completed firings.
The memo directed paid leave by January 22 and agencies to develop RIF actions, with later deadlines for implementation plans.

source_urls.access_notes: Official order signed January 20, 2025; text reviewed.
supports: The order directs agencies to terminate DEI offices and positions to the maximum extent allowed by law within 60 days, subject to applicable law and appropriations.

supported_facts: Trump signed an order on January 20, 2025 directing agencies to end federal DEI offices and positions within a period of up to 60 days, subject to law.
OPM's January 21 guidance directed staff onto paid leave by January 22 and required agencies to prepare reduction-in-force plans.
unsupported_original_claims: The source record does not show that every federal DEI officer was fired overnight on January 20.
The paid-leave and RIF steps were sequential and included future deadlines; they are not proof hundreds had already lost employment on January 20.
The cited sources do not document all described employee notices, union grievances, or legal challenges.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump order begins process to dismantle federal DEI offices and positions
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Trump signed an executive order on January 20, 2025 directing agencies to end DEI offices and positions within 60 days to the extent allowed by law. OPM then directed DEI office staff to paid leave by January 22 while agencies prepared reduction-in-force plans; the order did not document all staff being fired that night.

exact_evidence_gap: The sources establish a directive, leave deadline and future RIF process, but not that all DEI officers were terminated on January 20 or how many had actually lost employment by that date.
disposition_rationale: Distinguish the executive order, paid leave and planned future personnel actions from completed firings.

original_claim_summary: The administration allegedly eliminated all federal funding for Legal Services Corporation in February 2025, leaving civil legal aid organizations without support.

source_urls.access_notes: LSC statement dated May 30, 2025; includes FY2025 appropriation and the administration's FY2026 budget proposal.
supports: LSC said it received a $560 million FY2025 congressional appropriation.
The May 30 White House FY2026 budget proposal sought $21 million for close-out costs and proposed eliminating LSC.

source_urls.access_notes: LSC appropriation reference reviewed; it records enacted funding amounts.
supports: The appropriation history distinguishes enacted congressional funding from presidential budget requests.

source_urls.access_notes: LSC announcement dated January 8, 2026; reports Congress-passed FY2026 appropriation.
supports: Congress later enacted $540 million for LSC in FY2026, so the May 2025 proposal to eliminate LSC was not the final funding outcome.

supported_facts: LSC had $560 million in FY2025 congressional funding.
The Trump administration proposed eliminating LSC in its May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget request, with $21 million for close-out costs if approved.
Congress later provided $540 million for LSC in FY2026; therefore the administration proposal did not become a complete defunding.
unsupported_original_claims: The sources contradict a February 2025 elimination: LSC received FY2025 funding, and the elimination proposal appeared in the May 2025 FY2026 budget request.
A presidential budget proposal is not itself an enacted rescission or cancellation of existing grants.
The sources do not establish that legal-aid organizations had already lost all federal support or immediately ceased services.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump's FY2026 budget proposes eliminating the Legal Services Corporation
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: The White House proposed eliminating the Legal Services Corporation in its May 30, 2025 FY2026 budget request, including $21 million for close-out costs. LSC had received $560 million in FY2025, and Congress later provided $540 million for FY2026; the February claim of completed defunding is inaccurate.

exact_evidence_gap: No reviewed source supports a February defunding; the evidence shows existing FY2025 appropriations and a later FY2026 proposal that still required congressional action.
disposition_rationale: Report the funding proposal as proposed and distinguish it from enacted appropriations or completed service cuts.

original_claim_summary: The entry states as a settled legal fact that Trump violated the Foreign Emoluments Clause through foreign-government spending at his properties during his presidency.

source_urls.publisher: House Committee on Oversight and Accountability Democrats
source_urls.access_notes: The committee release and linked report were reviewed; characterize the figure as the committee's reported finding.
supports: The Democratic minority staff reported at least $7.8 million from 20 foreign governments through four Trump properties, based on records from two years of his presidency.

source_urls.access_notes: Official docket for Trump v. CREW, No. 20-330; disposition dated January 25, 2021.
supports: The Court vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss the case as moot after Trump left office; it did not decide the constitutional merits.

source_urls.access_notes: Official docket for Trump v. District of Columbia, No. 20-331; disposition dated January 25, 2021.
supports: The Court vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss as moot, not a merits finding of an Emoluments Clause violation.

supported_facts: House Oversight Democrats reported at least $7.8 million in payments from 20 foreign governments through four Trump properties, based on a limited set of records covering two years.
The cited Supreme Court emoluments cases were dismissed as moot after Trump left office; the Court did not issue a final merits ruling establishing a constitutional violation.
unsupported_original_claims: The House committee report is a Democratic minority staff finding and legal allegation; it is not a court judgment.
The Supreme Court dockets do not establish that the Foreign Emoluments Clause was violated on the merits.
The report's $7.8 million covers four named properties and two years of records, not every Trump entity, every payment, or all four years of the presidency.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: House Democrats report $7.8 million in foreign-government payments to Trump properties
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: House Oversight Democrats reported that records showed at least $7.8 million from 20 foreign governments flowed through four Trump properties during two years of his presidency. Emoluments litigation ended as moot after Trump left office and did not produce a final Supreme Court merits ruling establishing a violation.

exact_evidence_gap: The committee report supports a limited attributed payment finding and legal allegation; the court dockets show no merits adjudication of the constitutional claim.
disposition_rationale: Describe the payment amount with attribution and scope, and do not state a constitutional violation as judicially established.

original_claim_summary: The administration allegedly deported people in March 2025 because of years-old social-media posts criticizing U.S. policy.

source_urls.source_type: news reporting based on sources familiar with a DHS operation
source_urls.access_notes: Article text retrieved; reports a task force and potential visa-revocation screening, not completed deportations for old posts.
supports: NBC reported on April 9, 2025 that DHS was using data tools to review the social-media histories of an estimated 1.5 million foreign students for potential visa-revocation grounds.
The report said DHS was also considering activity it deemed antisemitic and physical harassment as grounds to revoke or deny immigration benefits.

source_urls.source_type: news reporting on DHS review methods
source_urls.access_notes: Article text retrieved; it describes a criminal-history records check for 1.3 million students and resulting hits, a separate process from social-media screening.
supports: DHS separately ran names of foreign-born students through a criminal-history index; this source does not establish deportation for old political posts.

supported_facts: NBC reported DHS was screening foreign students' social-media histories for potential grounds to revoke visas in April 2025.
The reporting describes screening and possible visa decisions, not a March policy or completed deportations for posts made years earlier.
unsupported_original_claims: No reviewed source establishes deportations in March specifically because of old social-media posts criticizing U.S. policy.
The NBC report concerns foreign-student screening in April and potential visa revocation; screening is not proof of a completed deportation or the reason for an individual case.
The sources do not establish the asserted retroactive punishment, unconstitutional conduct, or legal experts' conclusions as adjudicated findings.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: NBC reports DHS used social-media screening to review foreign students
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: NBC News reported on April 9, 2025 that a DHS task force was using data tools to review foreign students' social-media histories for potential grounds to revoke visas. The report did not establish that people were deported in March because of years-old posts criticizing U.S. policy.

exact_evidence_gap: The source does not identify an individual deportation caused by an old post, give a March event date, or establish that political criticism was the basis for a completed removal.
disposition_rationale: Use the narrower, attributed screening report and keep it separate from claims about completed deportations and individual speech-related cases.

original_claim_summary: The Trump administration allegedly ended habeas corpus for detained immigrants in March 2025 and directed officials to ignore petitions and transfer detainees around judges' orders.

source_urls.access_notes: Reuters article text reviewed; it reports May 14 public comments and consideration of a possible suspension.
supports: Kristi Noem said she believed recent levels of illegal immigration could provide a legal rationale to suspend habeas corpus.
Stephen Miller said the administration was actively looking at suspension; Reuters reports discussion, not implementation.

source_urls.access_notes: AP report text retrieved; describes Stephen Miller's public comments about the administration considering the option.
supports: The administration publicly discussed whether it could suspend habeas corpus; the report does not describe an enacted policy ending detainees' ability to petition courts.

supported_facts: On May 14, 2025, Noem said she believed recent illegal-immigration levels could justify a suspension; Miller had said the administration was actively considering it.
The reporting describes a possible suspension under discussion, not a March directive ending habeas protections.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited reporting does not establish that habeas corpus was ended in March 2025.
It does not report a policy directing immigration officials to ignore court petitions or transfer detainees to evade favorable rulings.
It does not establish multiple judges held officials in contempt over such a policy or that a constitutional crisis resulted.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Noem and Miller discuss possible habeas suspension in May 2025
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: In May 2025, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem said recent immigration levels could provide a legal rationale to suspend habeas corpus, and Stephen Miller said the administration was considering the option. The reports document discussion of a possible suspension, not an implemented March policy ending judicial review for detained immigrants.

exact_evidence_gap: The sources establish public consideration of a possible suspension but identify no order, implementation date, instruction to ignore petitions, or contempt ruling matching the original narrative.
disposition_rationale: Replace the asserted completed March action with the sourced May discussion and preserve the distinction between a proposal and an implemented restriction.

original_claim_summary: Donald Trump Jr. allegedly lobbied for Trump Organization business interests while working from the White House.

source_urls.access_notes: AP article text retrieved; published April 23, 2017 and directly reports the sons taking the helm and considering domestic expansion.
supports: The report concerns Eric and Donald Trump Jr. taking the helm of the Trump Organization during their father's presidency and the company's business plans.

supported_facts: AP reporting describes Eric and Donald Trump Jr. running the Trump Organization during Donald Trump's first presidency and looking toward domestic business expansion.
unsupported_original_claims: The cited report does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House.
It does not establish that he performed official White House duties or lobbied federal officials on behalf of Trump Organization while serving as a government employee.
The timing of the sons' business leadership during the presidency alone does not prove use of White House resources or an official role.

narrow_corrected_claim.title: Trump sons run family business during their father's first presidency
narrow_corrected_claim.claim: Associated Press reporting described Eric and Donald Trump Jr. taking the helm of the Trump Organization while their father was president and considering domestic expansion. The account does not establish that Donald Trump Jr. worked from the White House or held an official government position.

exact_evidence_gap: No reviewed source supports the specific 'working from White House' assertion or identifies a lobbying act, official capacity, date, or recipient tied to Trump Organization interests.
disposition_rationale: Retain only the sourced business-management context if useful; remove the unsupported White House-work and lobbying claim.
